opening.headline: To ensure that high-volume overnight jobs can be processed cheaply and critical requests can be reliably processed, you need to choose a processing level based on your tolerance for delay.
body: There are two tasks using the same model. One is the task of sorting out tens of thousands of inquiries at night, with results available hours later, but the unit cost must be low. The other is a consultative summary, where people are waiting, so delays should be short and constant.

In this class, we will look at what standard, batch, flex, priority and fast mode, and reserved capacity exchange. Practice judgment in selecting a processing level based on tolerance for delay, impact of failure, unit cost difference, and implementation burden.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the differences between batch, flex, and priority processing levels
Can provide a basis for selecting a processing level appropriate for delay tolerance

screens.title: Bulk work at night is done cheaply and important requests are done reliably.
screens.lead: Read on to compare two tasks within the same service. It's helpful to note how the demands of the two tasks differ.

visual.alt: Night bulk work and consultation summary side by side with two cards with different needs.
labels: Volume in the tens of thousands

paragraphs: In a certain service, two tasks use the same model. One is an overnight bulk operation that sorts tens of thousands of inquiries overnight. It doesn't matter if it takes a few hours, as the results only need to be available by morning. However, due to the large number of cases, even a small increase in unit price significantly increases the total cost.

The other is a consultation summary that agents need while on the phone with a customer. Because people are waiting, the delay must be short, and the jaggedness of sometimes being fast and sometimes being slow is also difficult. In this task, consistency of response is more important than unit cost.

The two tasks use the same model and the same API, but have diametrically opposite requirements. One wants it done cheaply instead of accepting a delay, and the other wants it done reliably, even if it means paying more. The question for this class is how can we have the same API handle these two differently?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What costs or problems would arise if both tasks were handled in the same basic way? I'll answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall from my experience which requests can and cannot wait.

screens.title: Think about it: Requests that can and cannot wait
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Which of the tasks you are currently running will not be a problem even if the results are an hour late?
items.answer: Typical tasks include assessment data generation, bulk classification, data enrichment, and report dictionary generation. These tasks are candidates for lower unit costs in exchange for accepting delays.

items.prompt: Conversely, what requests would cause users to bounce even if they were just a few seconds late?
items.answer: Requests like conversations, live support, or confirmation during payment that the user is waiting for in front of the screen. These requests require short and consistent delays, even if they cost slightly more.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced slowdowns in important requests during peak traffic?
items.answer: Public resources become crowded during peak hours. If important requests are in line with less important requests, they will be slowed down together. This is why you need priority or reserved capacity.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's first draw an overall map of the processing classes.

screens.title: Processing level maps: Standard, Batch, Flex, Priority, Reserved
screens.lead: Read the table to compare how processing levels trade off unit costs and delays.

visual.alt: A processing grade layout with delay tolerance on the horizontal axis and unit cost on the vertical axis.
labels: If you accept delays, the unit price goes down.

data.caption: Processing level comparison
rows: Gather requests and process them asynchronously
Typically 50% off, high limits, and 24-hour target completion time
Synchronous call but treated as low priority
Delays may be inconsistent and resources may be unavailable

Secure capacity even during peak times

data.notes: What you need to read in this map is the trade-off: lower-cost tiers give away delay or certainty, while short-latency, consistent tiers are more expensive. Since the name and detailed conditions of the level are different for each service, check the conditions for each service one by one on the following screens.

screens.outro: Now that we have drawn the map, we will compare the conditions for each service, starting with placement.

screens.title: Batch API condition comparison
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the terms and limitations of batch processing for each service.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini Batch API processes at 50% of the standard cost and has a target completion time of 24 hours. It usually ends sooner than that. Input supports two methods: Inline requests are written when the total size is less than 20MB, and JSONL input files are written when the total size is larger.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: The OpenAI Batch API offers a 50% discount and a separate, much higher rate limit, and targets completion within 24 hours. Each request requires a unique custom_id. The results are mapped to this identifier rather than the request order.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude Message Batches reduce costs by 50% and most are completed in under an hour. One batch can be up to 100,000 requests or 256MB. If it is not completed within 24 hours, it will expire, and results can be downloaded for 29 days after creation. Consider this expiration and storage period together when determining the timing.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: All three services offer asynchronous processing, unit cost savings of approximately 50%, and high limits. We assign a unique identifier to each request, check completion status, and match the result with the request by the identifier. For high-volume tasks that don't require an immediate response, this is the first choice to look at.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the deployment, let's compare Flex, which is cheaper and faster with synchronous calls, and Priority.

screens.title: Flex and Priority (Fast mode)
screens.lead: Compare Flex, which alternates between two states and chooses a lower unit price, and Priority, which chooses consistency at a higher unit price.

visual.alt: Two-line flowchart comparing the retry and demote behavior of Flex and Priority.

states.label: Flex (cheap and variable)
states.body: Gemini Flex specifies service_tier as flex and offers a 50% cost savings compared to standard. Instead, delays vary and availability is best effort. If resources are insufficient, you may receive a 429 or 503, and since there is no server-side fallback, the client must provide its own retry logic and a timeout of 10 minutes or more. Here, 429 is a status code that means that too many requests were sent in a standard specified time, and 503 is a status code that means that the server cannot process due to temporary overload or maintenance. Both responses can contain the wait time in a Retry-After header, which is an HTTP standard and not a feature of any particular service. If the value is present, retry after that time, if not, increase the interval and add a random delay. OpenAI Flex is calculated at a batch rate and is used for low-priority tasks such as evaluation, data enrichment, and asynchronous operations.

states.label: Priority·Fast mode (expensive and consistent)
states.body: Gemini Priority is processed before Standard and Flex, and traffic over the limit is gradually demoted to Standard without failing. Reduces the chance of important requests being unexpectedly rejected. OpenAI Fast mode provides up to 2.5x faster speeds and consistent latency, and specifies fast or priority as service_tier. Instead of making a profit, you pay a premium price.

screens.outro: Now that we have compared the two levels, let's look at the method of securing capacity in advance and Claude's Fast mode.

IETF RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (Section 10.2.3 Retry-After, Section 15.6.4 503 Service Unavailable)

screens.title: Reserved capacity and Fast mode
screens.lead: Move the slider to see what happens as you increase your reservation capacity.

stops.body: All requests are processed on a pay-as-you-go basis. This may be fine during normal times, but if there is insufficient capacity during peak times, even important requests can be delayed or limited. If traffic is constant and low, this is sufficient.

OpenAI Reserved Tier buys dollar-per-minute capacity per model in advance to reserve capacity even during peak times. Standard and Fast requests within the reservation limit are processed as reservations, ensuring reliable processing even during peak times.

Any excess over the reservation limit will be charged at a pay-as-you-go rate. Therefore, if there are insufficient reservations, your request will not be failed; instead, some will be processed at regular rates and under regular conditions. Additionally, Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage, so reservations are for Standard and Fast requests.

Claude Fast mode sets the speed to fast to run the same model in a faster configuration. Up to 2.5x output token speed and premium pricing. The gain is focused on output speed rather than time to first token, making it suitable for requests that need to complete long responses quickly.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the nature of the grades, let's look at the judgment of choosing a placement in an example.

screens.title: Illustrative example: Batch tasks that do not require an immediate response
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Tens of thousands of inquiries need to be sorted overnight and the resulting evaluation dataset needs to be created. The results are used at the meeting the next morning. If you send the same model through standard processing, both the limit and the cost will be burdensome.

steps.title: Step 1: Check your delay tolerance
steps.body: Since the results only need to be available by morning, the tolerance for delay is high. No people are waiting, and even if some requests are late, the overall schedule is not affected. This is the first condition under which placement can be considered.

steps.title: Step 2: Collect and send requests
steps.body: Gather the requests into a JSONL-like file, send it in batches, and attach a unique identifier to each request. Gemini and OpenAI take file input, and Claude supports up to 100,000 requests or 256MB per batch, so we split them by size.

steps.title: Step 3: Check completion and match results
steps.body: Check completion status periodically. Because the results may differ from the request order, an identifier matches the results to the original request. We also prepare a procedure to select and resend only failed requests. If some requests fail, there is no need to resend the entire batch.

steps.title: Step 4: Consider effect and timing
steps.body: The expected benefits are approximately 50% unit cost savings and higher limits. Since your batch may expire if not completed within 24 hours and results have a limited retention period, count backwards from your morning meeting time and submit in the late afternoon or evening.

steps.title: Let's check together
steps.body: Human pending requests, such as consultation summaries, are not mixed into this batch. The conclusion of this case is that even within the same service, grades are divided according to the nature of the request.

screens.outro: Now that I've decided which tasks to send in batches, I'll summarize the basis for choosing a grade.

screens.title: Explanatory Example: Basis for Selecting Delay Tolerance Road Grades
screens.lead: When you select each situation, the grade and rationale chosen by the instructor are revealed. Choose it yourself first and then unfold it. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: Which tier is right for high-volume jobs that can tolerate delays of several hours?
items.answer: It's a batch. You get a discount of about 50%, higher limits, and just accept the implementation burden of asynchronous processing and polling. Unit cost efficiency is best when delay tolerance is highest.

items.prompt: Want to tolerate seconds to minutes of delay and reduce costs?
items.answer: Review Flex. Since it is a synchronous call, the implementation is simple, but since 429 or 503 may occur, retries and long timeouts are required. It's only appropriate if you can bear that burden.

items.prompt: What if your users are waiting and you need a consistent response?
items.answer: Standard or Priority and Fast mode. If the delay must be short and constant, pay a premium price and use Priority or Fast mode. This is because the value of user experience is greater than unit price. Again, you can save money by applying it only to those that are truly delay-sensitive, rather than to all requests.

items.prompt: What if you expect a surge in traffic and securing it is important?
items.answer: Review reserved capacity. Buy capacity in advance to ensure throughput even during peak times. However, it does not apply to Batch or Flex, so it is a choice for standard and fast requests.

items.prompt: How should I present the basis for this choice?
items.answer: We present it in four ways. Tolerance of delay, impact of failure, difference in unit cost, and implementation burden. For example, batches have high latency tolerance and large cost differences, but polling must be implemented. Write down all four items.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized the evidence, let's gather the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Expand items to see evidence
screens.lead: When you select each item, the basis for the summary statement will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.title: Delay tolerance is the first criterion for selecting a processing level.
items.body: The first question to ask is how late you can expect to receive your results. The unit price goes down as you accept the delay, and the shorter and more consistent the delay, the higher the unit price.

items.title: Batch is cheap, bulk, and asynchronous; Flex is cheap, variable, and synchronous processing.
items.body: The batch offers around 50% discount and high limits, but look up the results later. Flex is a synchronous call, but it can throw a 429 or 503, requiring retries and long timeouts.

items.title: Priority and Fast modes cost more to gain latency and consistency.
items.body: Gemini Priority is processed first, and excesses are gradually demoted. OpenAI Fast mode and Claude Fast mode provide up to 2.5x speed at a premium price.

items.title: Reserved capacity is an advance purchase to secure peak times and does not apply to Batch and Flex.
items.body: Capacity is purchased in advance in dollars per minute for each model, Standard and Fast requests within the limit are reserved, and excesses are billed on a pay-as-you-go basis.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this class are batch API, Flex processing, Priority processing, and reserved capacity. Let's go back to the original question. How can nightly bulk tasks and consultation summaries be processed differently using the same API?
You can send nightly bulk work in batches, and consultation summaries as standard or priority. The difference between the two tasks is not the model, but how much delay it can tolerate.
List the requests you operate in order of delay tolerance. If you write down the requests you allow in hours, minutes, and seconds, you can see which requests correspond to which level.

Then check the implementation burden of writing that rating. Batch requires polling and identifier matching, Flex requires retries and long timeouts. Change levels when the unit cost difference is greater than the implementation burden. After making changes, measure the actual delay and failure rate to see if your decision was correct.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does my job get stuck with the batch API? Think about whether there are tasks you are handling now that are standard, but can be delayed by a few hours. Conversely, also check to see if there are requests that require more consistent responses to be handled by the standard.

checks.q: Match the following processing levels with personality:
right: Buy capacity in advance and secure it even during peak times.
Get low latency and consistency at a premium price
Requests are collected and processed asynchronously, usually at a 50% discount.
It is a synchronous call, but it is cheaper, but the delay is variable and availability is best effort.
checks.explain: Processing level trades delay tolerance and unit price. Accept delays and uncertainty for cheap processing, and go for more expensive tiers if you need consistent delays.
checks.intro: Processing levels trade off unit cost and delay tolerance. Match grades with personality.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You've correctly distinguished between cheap but slow or uncertain grades and expensive but consistent grades.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Batch and synchronous processing are asynchronous, but Flex provides variable delay, and Priority provides consistency at a premium price.

checks.q: Sort bulk inquiries into batches in order of processing
items: Check the delay tolerance to see if the results only need to come out by morning.
Gather requests into a JSONL-like file and send them in batches with a unique request identifier.
Match the result to the request with an identifier
checks.explain: Since placement is asynchronous, delay tolerance is considered first. Results are matched by identifier rather than request order, and the timing is determined considering expiration and result storage period.
checks.intro: Sequence the process for processing bulk sorting in batches.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. You established the flow of checking delay tolerance, submitting with an identifier, polling the status, and responding to the results with the identifier.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. Since batching is asynchronous, check the allowable delay first, and make sure that the results are matched to the request by identifier, not by order.

checks.q: In one service, there is a consultation summary that people wait for, and an overnight bulk triage that only ends by morning. What is the right combination of grades?
options: Both are sent in batches to keep the unit cost as low as possible.
Consultation summary is processed as Flex, night classification is processed as Priority.
Consultation summaries are processed as standard or priority, and night classification is processed in batches.
Both are sent to Flex and processed without retry logic.
checks.explain: Delay tolerance is the first criterion. Human-awaited requests require consistent responses, and bulk operations that tolerate delays of several hours require batch discounts and high limits.

wrong.0: The consultation summary cannot be written after a few hours.
wrong.1: Flex, which has inconsistent delays, is not suitable for requests that people are waiting for, and using expensive priority for night work is a waste.
wrong.3: Flex can return 429 or 503, which requires retries and long timeouts, and is not suitable for human-waiting requests.

checks.intro: Even within the same service, each request has different delay tolerances. Choose the right combination of levels.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Requests that people are waiting for require consistent responses, and tasks that only need to be completed by morning use batch discounts.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The first criterion is delay tolerance. The combination of sending human-waiting requests to classes with jagged delays, or processing all tasks in the same class, does not fit the two needs together.

glossary.def: Requests are aggregated and processed asynchronously, typically offering a 50% discount and completion within 24 hours.
A class of synchronous processing that is cheaper than standard but has variable delays and may be out of resources.
This tier provides higher priority and consistent latency at a premium price. OpenAI also uses Fast mode.
This method secures throughput even during peak times by purchasing capacity in advance for each model.
This mode increases output speed by running the same model in a faster configuration. Up to 2.5x faster and comes with a premium price.

misconceptions.myth: Batch is simply sending requests all at once.
misconceptions.fact: Batches are processed asynchronously and results are retrieved later. Instead, the unit price is low and the limit is high.

misconceptions.myth: Flex is slow, but always succeeds.
misconceptions.fact: If you are short on resources, you may get 429 or 503. Clients must implement retry logic and long timeouts themselves.
For Claude, the gain is concentrated in output speed and not in reduced time to first token.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Delay tolerance is the first criterion for selecting a processing level.
Batch is cheap, bulky, and asynchronous, and Flex is cheap, but volatile, synchronous processing.
Priority and Fast modes pay more to get lower latency and consistency.
Reserved capacity is an advance purchase to secure peak times and does not apply to Batch and Flex.
